title: catástrofe orquestra #1 (Ato I)
text: That is what a catastrophe is: everything comes crashing down. A catastrophe is never the final silence, but the exact moment when matter under stress is forced to emit its strongest and deepest frequency. My questions have been heading in exactly that direction: how can we orchestrate a great ruin? How can we understand the way in which we are able to compose the very collapse of the world, of life, and of death?

title: catástrofe orquestra #1 (Ato I)
text: The history of humanity is like a great battle of materialities. When I received the invitation from the Bienal, it was a great opportunity to reflect on the materials I’ve been researching and how they might collide with one another, generating friction. The matchboxes that carry fire. Coal, which is essentially a fossilized, burned tree; which fueled industrial production in the past century; which brought us to our current technological model—driven and shaped by the historical rhythms that fire (and water) have created over time. In catástrofe orquestra #1 (Ato I), I am interested in the violent act of the coal pendulums being dropped onto the drum as a representation of this historical thread.
speaker: Antonio Társis
source: "Catastrophe orchestra: an interview with Antonio Társis", Fundação Bienal de São Paulo

title: catástrofe orquestra #1 (Ato I)
text: I sought to compose these relationships with materials and historical events: extraction, which transforms matter into technology; technology, which reorganizes behaviors, emotions, ways of life, and violence. One thing overlapping another, like a massive fire having a domino effect or a large orchestra in which each instrument has its own function and note. The catastrophe ceases to be an isolated event and comes to be seen as a functioning system, governing our lives at every moment.

title: Homo Machina (Human Machine, a.k.a. Gay Machine)
text: We are on the edge of a new era. If technology is the medium of the future, it cannot be separated from class, fantasy, labor, and the body. title: Homo Machina (Human Machine, a.k.a. Gay Machine)

title: Homo Machina (Human Machine, a.k.a. Gay Machine)

title: No Bird
text: The origins of this work lay in imagining these now-vanished flightless birds. Perhaps they might have survived if their footsteps were erased?
speaker: UJOO+LIMHEEYOUNG
source: No Bird, work description on the artists' blog, January 2026

title: No Bird
text: The repetitive cycle of these two machines—endlessly leaving and erasing—reveals a state in which action is continuously produced yet exhausted without leading to any change or direction.
speaker: UJOO+LIMHEEYOUNG
source: No Bird, work description on the artists' blog, January 2026

title: No Bird
text: This serves as a metaphor for the conditions of a post-automation society, where humans remain alive but exist as beings unable to intervene in the world.
speaker: UJOO+LIMHEEYOUNG
source: No Bird, work description on the artists' blog, January 2026

title: No Bird
text: What vanishes is not only the flightless bird. What is disappearing is the human role, no longer summoned in a post-automation society, along with the conditions of meaning and dignity that humans have given to themselves.
speaker: UJOO+LIMHEEYOUNG
source: Catalogue text, Prix Ars Electronica 2026 (Honorary Mention, Interactive Art +)

title: No Bird
text: Through its physical mechanical structure, No Bird asks what it means to exist as a human in a post-technological era, and how we might live beyond mere survival.
speaker: UJOO+LIMHEEYOUNG
source: Catalogue text, Prix Ars Electronica 2026 (Honorary Mention, Interactive Art +)

title: NoSearchBar
text: A distinction can be made between specific and non-specific software-related data access: The specific search hardly has any surprises in store, due to its purpose of existence. We find what we are looking for, the problems, preferences, and needs are specifically individual, predominantly environmental, and self-driven.
speaker: Erik Anton Reinhardt
source: Prix Ars Electronica 2022 winners page, project text (archived)

title: NoSearchBar
text: Examples of this are forecast systems, sorting, categories, and recommendation systems, which try to anticipate users’ problems, preferences, and needs but often also to create new ones.
speaker: Erik Anton Reinhardt
source: Prix Ars Electronica 2022 winners page, project text (archived)

title: NoSearchBar
text: By removing the SearchBar, we are exposed to an ideological software anticipation. We no longer have the opportunity to articulate our own problems, preferences, and needs but are always left with mixed feelings between frustration and hope that the right thing could still emerge.
speaker: Erik Anton Reinhardt
source: Prix Ars Electronica 2022 winners page, project text (archived)

title: NoSearchBar
text: The specific access is reflected in the way we articulate ourselves through using a SearchBar. We find the answers to our needs and problems that are driven by an individual's desires.
speaker: Erik Anton Reinhardt
source: UdK Berlin New Media Class, student project page

title: Nothing to See Here
text: We playfully challenge you to consider what is true or real, and whether we can ever truly know.
speaker: Celine Daemen
source: Statement on Nothing to see here, Studio Nergens website (English version)

title: Nothing to See Here
text: Fragmented truths in endless doomscrolling, AI videos of cute but non-existent cats, fake news reports – reality is not one fixed fact, but something relational that comes into being in the interaction between our body, the other and the space,
speaker: Celine Daemen
source: Quoted in 'Nothing to see here', Creative Industries Fund NL project page

title: Nothing to See Here
text: By literally positioning someone opposite themselves, I hope to force the audience to rethink that relationship for a moment.
speaker: Celine Daemen
source: Quoted in 'Nothing to see here', Creative Industries Fund NL project page

title: Nothing to See Here
text: To see a group of strangers of different ages and backgrounds having a chat and while doing so asking the question whether we actually agree on what is real, I find that moving and important in these times,
speaker: Celine Daemen
source: Quoted in 'Nothing to see here', Creative Industries Fund NL project page

title: Nothing to See Here
text: I hope a lot more people will put their heads into this peep-show box for a moment, only to emerge somewhat confused and dazed. That they look at the world around them with new eyes.
speaker: Celine Daemen
source: Quoted in 'Nothing to see here', Creative Industries Fund NL project page

title: Now You See Me, Now You Don't
text: Puddles are humble, beautiful things, and they used to have a longer life on Earth
speaker: Manal AlDowayan
source: The National, 'Saudi artist Manal AlDowayan unveils new piece of land art addressing water scarcity in Al Ula' (2020)

title: Now You See Me, Now You Don't
text: Al Ula was founded because it had plentiful springs, it was this oasis in the desert, but as the climate changed these local communities had to start tapping into the underground reserves, so even when it does rain, puddles disappear almost instantly.
speaker: Manal AlDowayan
source: The National (2020)

title: Now You See Me, Now You Don't
text: I wanted kids to engage, as they might jump in a puddle. At night the work is up-lit and appears as strange black pools. People are nervous at first, but I've seen young and old now have a go.
speaker: Manal AlDowayan
source: The National (2020)

title: Now You See Me, Now You Don't
text: I work in a lot of different media, my projects always take different forms, and have different politics, but ideas of disappearance and invisibility run through everything I do.
speaker: Manal AlDowayan
source: The National (2020)

title: Nuestra Victoria (Our Victory)
text: The work consists of a 3D digital archive that intends to preserve the data of the monument after its occupation by civil society.
speaker: Julieta Gil
source: Nuestra Victoria, project text on the artist's website

title: Nuestra Victoria (Our Victory)
text: The intention was not to make a perfect replica, but to also allow the materiality of this digital version to show through and reveal new layers of information about its process of preservation and restoration, and allow the mistakes and imperfections of the scan to serve as a metaphor for the fragility of patriarchal institutions.
speaker: Julieta Gil
source: Nuestra Victoria, project text on the artist's website

title: Nuestra Victoria (Our Victory)
text: Hours after the protest, government censorship prevented people from seeing the Angel of Independence by boarding it up and immediately working on its restoration, thus erasing all the claims against violence that were posted by women all over the monument. This work allows the words and actions of protest to remain in our collective memory.
speaker: Julieta Gil
source: Lumen Prize Gold Award winner 2020, work description

title: Nyctinasty
text: It references both bodily and symbolic practices of caring for the body and spirit after death, forging a vital link between the living and the dead.
speaker: Hayley Millar Baker
source: Nyctinasty, artist's website

title: Nyctinasty
text: In this context, death is seen not as an end but as a continuation within the spiritual realm, reflecting a timeless link to ancestral wisdom and spiritual continuity.
speaker: Hayley Millar Baker
source: Nyctinasty, artist's website

title: Nyctinasty
text: Nyctinasty illuminates female power and strength, shifting away from the horror genre’s emphasis on women's psychosis. The Indigenous female body is depicted not as a victim but as a vessel bearing practices of magic and spirituality rooted in millennia of tradition.
speaker: Hayley Millar Baker
source: Nyctinasty, artist's website

title: Nyctinasty
text: I wouldn’t say I’m reclaiming Indigenous history through my art just because it wasn’t unclaimed – it’s always been ours and has always belonged to us regardless of whether the mainstream choose to learn or tell it.
speaker: Hayley Millar Baker
source: RUSSH, 'Bare bones: Hayley Millar Baker on separating memory from experience' (Elyssa Kostopoulos), 19 April 2022

title: Nyctinasty
text: At the end of the day, I am making work about me, but if I can extend that to bring others into my narrative as if it were relating or reflecting to a story of their own, what a wonderful way to connect.
speaker: Hayley Millar Baker
source: RUSSH, 'Bare bones: Hayley Millar Baker on separating memory from experience' (Elyssa Kostopoulos), 19 April 2022

title: Oceans in Transformation
text: The oceans are changing very fast, yet knowledge of them is moving slowly and is enveloped in long-established forms of cultural separation and distinction between human activities at land and at sea. This division needs to be rethought to address the urgent and vast transformations that the seas are undergoing.
speaker: Territorial Agency
source: TBA21, Territorial Agency: Oceans in Transformation exhibition page

title: Oceans in Transformation
text: The ocean is a sensorium, an aesthetic device: it records in its complex dynamics the transformations of the Earth, and it inscribes back its cycles in the dynamics of life-forms. Oceans in Transformation is an aesthetic and conceptual setting, where different ways of being sensitive to the complex events of climate change are brought into close proximity.
speaker: Territorial Agency (project description)
source: S+T+ARTS Prize 2021 project page

title: Oceans in Transformation
text: Oceans in Transformation is organized by large dynamic compositions of remote sensing images where the gaps between different knowledge components, areas with no data and areas with contradictory and ambiguous understanding are highlighted and brought to the forefront.
speaker: Territorial Agency (project description)
source: S+T+ARTS Prize 2021 project page

title: Oceans in Transformation
text: When within water, however, a multiplicity of refractions and echoes reorient our gridded understanding of the worlds we inhabit. How is agency distributed? Who and what can own?
speaker: John Palmesino, Ann-Sofi Rönnskog
source: When Above, e-flux Architecture, Oceans in Transformation

title: Oceans in Transformation
text: How are we to understand the current sets of transformations changing the ocean without reverting to an all-sweeping new horizon, one single line of sight? How to become alert to the multiple refractions and circulations that are coupled in the making of the Anthropocene ocean? How to think anew the relations between polities and their horizons? How to inscribe the discourses of territoriality into the multiple circulations of the ocean? How can we think from and with the ocean?
speaker: John Palmesino, Ann-Sofi Rönnskog
source: When Above, e-flux Architecture, Oceans in Transformation

title: Octopocalypse
text: With Octopocalypse, we explore a new form of filmmaking: cinematic narrative as an immersive, musical and interactive system, where image, sound, choice and presence become one live story engine.
speaker: Max Sacker, Arite Szadkowski
source: Main Creators' Statement, La Biennale di Venezia, Venice Immersive 2026

title: Octopocalypse
text: Generative AI is not used as a shortcut or an author, but as a tool that lets filmmakers prototype, refine and realise worlds, characters, voices and scenes with new speed and flexibility. The emotional intention, rhythm and point of view remain human.
speaker: Max Sacker, Arite Szadkowski
source: Main Creators' Statement, La Biennale di Venezia, Venice Immersive 2026

title: Octopocalypse
text: The installation asks participants to choose between extraction and trust, between preserving the status quo and imagining a more empathetic future.
speaker: Max Sacker, Arite Szadkowski
source: Main Creators' Statement, La Biennale di Venezia, Venice Immersive 2026

title: Octopocalypse
text: It asks whether humanity can recognise intelligence in a being it is tempted to treat as a resource.
speaker: Max Sacker, Arite Szadkowski
source: Synopsis, La Biennale di Venezia, Venice Immersive 2026

title: Of Men and Gods and Mud
text: At Venice Biennale, a new three channel video installation entitled 'Of Men and Gods and Mud' was made from images that I shot mainly on a brickyard in Sudan.
speaker: Ali Cherri
source: Artbreath interview

title: Of Men and Gods and Mud
text: It speaks of the mythologies around mud and the diverse religious beliefs of creation through it. Whether we refer to the biblical figure Adam, Enkidu, Golem, or so many other religious or mythological figures, humanity saw clay as the material of creation, where life came through mud.
speaker: Ali Cherri
source: Artbreath interview

title: Of Men and Gods and Mud
text: Mud has a dual aspect; destruction or deluge happens a lot along the Nile, where muddy waters rise up, destroy and can even kill people, but mud is also the fertiliser that permits for the earth to prosper.
speaker: Ali Cherri
source: Artbreath interview

title: Of Men and Gods and Mud
text: I work with imagination as a political strategy and tool for change,
speaker: Ali Cherri
source: Canvas, profile (Canvas 109)

title: Of Men and Gods and Mud
text: Mud has the ability to hold or break. It is the material manifestation of violence, of trauma, of loss, but also of sedimentation and prosperity. Mud can be an entry point for reconstruction histories, especially histories of violence.
speaker: Ali Cherri
source: BOMB, interview with Dina A. Ramadan (2023), reposted by Swiss Institute

title: Oikeiōsis
text: The world is loud with reasons to turn away from one another. I wanted to make quiet work. Not a protest, not a commentary, but a space where strangers can sit together and remember that this, too, is real.
speaker: Pavlina Vagioni
source: Quoted in 'Pavlina Vagioni Oikeiōsis: A Greek Artist Asks Venice to Remember How to Belong', Artlyst, 2026

title: Oikeiōsis
text: In a Biennale composed in the minor keys, this is the frequency I wanted to tune to: not a sound, but what the sound reveals.
speaker: unattributed (first person, in exhibition announcement)
source: Exhibition announcement, Hellenic Diaspora Foundation, e-flux

title: Oikeiōsis
text: In essence, I am not interested in retelling a myth, but in creating the conditions for an encounter with it—allowing the viewer to come into contact with what the myth reveals about human experience.
speaker: Pavlina Vagioni
source: Interview, Greek News Agenda

title: Oikeiōsis
text: Having studied classical singing for over a decade, I use my voice not as a vehicle for musical performance, but as material that connects sound to body and space.
speaker: Pavlina Vagioni
source: Interview, Greek News Agenda

title: Oikeiōsis
text: For me, material is never neutral. Every material carries meaning, whether through direct reference or symbolic resonance.
speaker: Pavlina Vagioni
source: Interview, Greek News Agenda

title: On a Clear Day You Can See Forever
text: In one take, without a single cut, I document every inch of the island from one edge to the other.
speaker: Tan Pin Pin
source: Tan Pin Pin, 'A filming manifesto for 80km/h', artist website

title: On a Clear Day You Can See Forever
text: I maintain a consistent speed of 80 km/h so the document retains cartographic value. If the same route along the Pan Island Expressway were recorded every year, Singapore’s topographical changes could be mapped by comparing recordings over time. It is my intention to film this journey regularly.
speaker: Tan Pin Pin
source: Tan Pin Pin, 'A filming manifesto for 80km/h', artist website

title: On a Clear Day You Can See Forever
text: This cross-country document lasts a mere 38 minutes. Its duration is its message.
speaker: Tan Pin Pin
source: Tan Pin Pin, 'A filming manifesto for 80km/h', artist website

title: Once Upon a Garden
text: Once Upon A Garden became a dystopian projection of a likely outcome of global warming where all plants and flowers from the West Africa region have disappeared from Earth. It depicted a reality where humans have to live with simulated images of these plants and flowers, based on a patchy digital memory of them.
speaker: Linda Dounia Rebeiz
source: It's Nice That, essay by the artist, 1 November 2023

title: Once Upon a Garden
text: This body of work also became an allegory for the lossy reflection of our humanity by AI. What we don’t include in training today contributes to a much hazier and incomplete understanding of our world.
speaker: Linda Dounia Rebeiz
source: It's Nice That, essay by the artist, 1 November 2023

title: Once Upon a Garden
text: The series also exposes just how poorly we are recording the extensive loss of wildlife, especially in certain parts of the world. This brings us back to a more general issue we have with the data we use to train AI—it’s missing or overlooking a great deal.
speaker: Linda Dounia
source: AI Art Questionnaire (Anika Meier), interview

title: Once Upon a Garden
text: In the first installment of the project, Once Upon a Garden, I didn't need to do anything to the images themselves, aside from using collage, because they were exactly as I expected them to be. They were spectral, ill-formed and weird-looking.
speaker: Linda Dounia
source: Le Random, interview with Peter Bauman, 19 February 2024

title: Once Upon a Garden
text: What plants did my grandmother see that I'm not seeing,
speaker: Linda Dounia
source: Google Arts & Culture, 'What Did Flowers Used To Look Like?'

title: Ongoing, Individual Adaptability or How to Quiet Quit
text: I thought the result would show something like the lowest common denominator and, above all, the architecture of the exhibition spaces. But the result was much more complex and interesting.
speaker: Devin Kenny
source: Interview with Pia-Marie Remmers, Galerie Elisabeth & Klaus Thoman, for 'Shake-Up Environment', 2023

title: Ongoing, Individual Adaptability or How to Quiet Quit
text: It was relatively difficult to get them, because the Whitney was worried that I would create something that would make the museum look bad or misrepresent the artists.
speaker: Devin Kenny
source: Interview with Pia-Marie Remmers, Galerie Elisabeth & Klaus Thoman, for 'Shake-Up Environment', 2023

title: Ongoing, Individual Adaptability or How to Quiet Quit
text: That was the idea! I wanted to collaborate, as much as possible, with the AI. This was before the hype and mass proliferation of AI image generators that we’ve seen this year. But I would not say it’s collaboration in the sense of working as equals. I feed the AI certain materials, it’s not free to choose, and it’s not free to stop collaborating.
speaker: Devin Kenny
source: Interview with Pia-Marie Remmers, Galerie Elisabeth & Klaus Thoman, for 'Shake-Up Environment', 2023

title: Ongoing, Individual Adaptability or How to Quiet Quit
text: It was a privilege for me to have access to these personal letters and I wanted to protect the relationships that unfolded before me. By the way, this is a similar process to sampling in HipHop, where existing audio is used in a different way.
speaker: Devin Kenny
source: Interview with Pia-Marie Remmers, Galerie Elisabeth & Klaus Thoman, for 'Shake-Up Environment', 2023

title: OPERA
text: Opera definitely started from the subject matter. I wanted to showcase a reflection of human society and history — I immediately thought about what would be the best way to convey our life, and realized that maybe following the conventional, linear narrative structure may not be the best way.
speaker: Erick Oh
source: Erick Oh On ‘Opera’ (Oscar Shorts Interview Series), Cartoon Brew, April 2021

title: OPERA
text: Conventional film language has the beginning and the end, a climax. History doesn’t work that way. Our life is one continuous rhythm, so that’s why I came up with this structure of the cycle, so we can watch this numerous times and embrace everything happening.
speaker: Erick Oh
source: Cartoon Brew, Oscar Shorts Interview Series, 2021

title: OPERA
text: Then the other one — that doesn’t have any camera movement — you just walk in, you see this huge pyramid structure. And then it’s really up to you to walk around and get closer and see the ending and the beginnings of each section all blended together.
speaker: Erick Oh
source: Cartoon Brew, Oscar Shorts Interview Series, 2021

title: OPERA
text: I think it simply comes from looking at the world and cycles of life and knowing you can’t control it. It constantly evolves and changes and transforms, and comes back to where it used to be.
speaker: Erick Oh
source: Cartoon Brew, Oscar Shorts Interview Series, 2021

title: OPERA
text: “Opera” itself doesn’t give you any answer. It’s almost like a mirror to ourselves. In the piece, you’ll find the world, all the social issues we are suffering with, life and death and eventually yourself. “Opera” doesn’t spoon feed you the message of hope. But it’ll have to be you who should take a moment to think and find a way to break out of this vicious cycle of repetitive history and make the world better.
speaker: Erick Oh
source: Interview with Jackson Murphy, Animation Scoop (email Q&A), 2021

title: Pandemonium
text: When I thought of this information maelstrom, what ultimately came to mind was constructing a collapsing tornado in the built environment, within a 360-degree surround space.
speaker: Michelle Lopez
source: Whitney Biennial catalogue conversation between Michelle Lopez and Christopher Y. Lew (artist's website)

title: Pandemonium
text: Because the original format was sited within a planetarium, I wanted to create my own constellations out of culture.
speaker: Michelle Lopez
source: Whitney Biennial catalogue conversation between Michelle Lopez and Christopher Y. Lew (artist's website)

title: Pandemonium
text: this project also came from another material I was thinking about: the internet and the amount of information and storage we have, more stuff. What could that look like in a work of art? How could I describe that outsize aspect of our world right now?
speaker: Michelle Lopez
source: Whitney Biennial catalogue conversation between Michelle Lopez and Christopher Y. Lew (artist's website)

title: Pandemonium
text: There's this moment at the end of the film where the debris all gets sucked away and disappears into blackness. I think a part of it is a sense of: Could there possibly be liberation from this world of stuff and from whatever systems we're all caught up in?
speaker: Michelle Lopez
source: Whitney Biennial catalogue conversation between Michelle Lopez and Christopher Y. Lew (artist's website)

title: Pandemonium
text: The work that I've been making now for about a decade has had to do with this sense of global collapse that I'm feeling.
speaker: Michelle Lopez
source: Whitney Biennial catalogue conversation between Michelle Lopez and Christopher Y. Lew (artist's website)

title: Paper Tears
text: I didn’t want to address these issues in a moralistic or reactionary way, which is why I chose the watermark as a medium: a margin on the page, a space open enough to play, struggle, and even bring joy.
speaker: Claudia Pagès Rabal
source: Fakewhale Log, 'Fakewhale in Dialogue with Claudia Pagès Rabal', 15 May 2026

title: Paper Tears
text: The watermarks I’ve chosen date back to the 15th century, a century marked by the expulsion of Jews and Arabs from the Iberian Peninsula and the colonization of the Americas. I probably chose this period to help me cope with the violence we see every day in today’s world.
speaker: Claudia Pagès Rabal
source: Fakewhale Log, 'Fakewhale in Dialogue with Claudia Pagès Rabal', 15 May 2026

title: Paper Tears
text: The figure of the jester and the use of humor seemed to me the only starting point from which we could approach this material without viewing it through a moral lens, and instead work with it from a place of joy.
speaker: Claudia Pagès Rabal
source: Fakewhale Log, 'Fakewhale in Dialogue with Claudia Pagès Rabal', 15 May 2026

title: Paper Tears
text: Just as the watermarks navigate in the negative and are only visible against the light, the water in the aquifers is also latent and only becomes visible when it is exploited, extracted.
speaker: Claudia Pagès Rabal
source: Fakewhale Log, 'Fakewhale in Dialogue with Claudia Pagès Rabal', 15 May 2026

title: Paper Tears
text: My works are time machines because they travel from the past to the present and back again.
speaker: Claudia Pagès Rabal
source: Fakewhale Log, 'Fakewhale in Dialogue with Claudia Pagès Rabal', 15 May 2026

title: Pinktoned (Exploded View)
text: These 1976 images are juxtaposed with my own contemporary footage of passersby filmed out the window of my East Hollywood studio. Photographed in close up detail, these images show gestures of figures on the street; tapping out texts on touch screens, flicking ash off the end of a cigarette, gripping a coffee cup, passing money for bus fare.
speaker: Mike Stoltz
source: EXiS (Experimental Film and Video Festival in Seoul), Pinktoned programme page

title: Pinktoned (Exploded View)
text: Originally conceived as an installation for the Made in LA Biennial at the Hammer Museum, Pinktoned is a meditative passage through the streets of Los Angeles and a rumination on how moving images function amidst paranoia and state violence.
speaker: Mike Stoltz
source: EXiS (Experimental Film and Video Festival in Seoul), Pinktoned programme page

title: Pinktoned (Exploded View)
text: Working with the physical medium, every time you make a cut it becomes harder and harder to repair that. There’s not an undo button the way there is on the timeline of Adobe Premiere or Final Cut. Every edit is very deliberate and very final,
speaker: Mike Stoltz
source: Binghamton News, 'Turning sounds into sights'

title: Pinktoned (Exploded View)
text: I view sound recording as my sketchbook practice. With moving images, I usually need downtime between shooting. There are also many similarities between using cassette tape and shooting on film. They are both linear, tactile mediums.
speaker: Mike Stoltz
source: Clint Enns, 'Re-Imagined Space: An Interview with Mike Stoltz', INCITE! (2014)

title: Pixel Dust
text: I am always thinking about what underlying structures are at work.
speaker: Leo Villareal
source: In Conversation with Leo Villareal, interview by Jeff Davis, Art Blocks, 20 Jan 2022 (answer about Cosmic Reef)

title: Pixel Dust
text: I am very intrigued by how very complex things can actually be described with a very simple program. I am also interested in the universal human responses to such systems.
speaker: Leo Villareal
source: In Conversation with Leo Villareal, interview by Jeff Davis, Art Blocks, 20 Jan 2022 (answer about Cosmic Reef)

title: Pixel Dust
text: I really like the open-ended nature of abstraction and how it allows for highly subjective responses in viewers. I find it refreshing to not see an image or text and for a work to be able to maintain a sense of mystery.
speaker: Leo Villareal
source: In Conversation with Leo Villareal, interview by Jeff Davis, Art Blocks, 20 Jan 2022

title: Pixel Dust
text: My work is also about time and a constant evolution and change. There is no beginning, middle, or end. Just a constant flow that a viewer can engage with or not, completely on their terms.
speaker: Leo Villareal
source: In Conversation with Leo Villareal, interview by Jeff Davis, Art Blocks, 20 Jan 2022

title: PL'AI
text: The point of departure was the question: what would it mean to make an artificial intelligence (AI) that thinks of itself as a plant? This idea is derived from my curiosity about the wider relationship between people and plants as well as the increasing use of machine learning algorithms that inform our understanding of the world.
speaker: Špela Petrič
source: "PL'AI: where plant and machine playfully meet", Waag

title: PL'AI
text: I wanted to reframe our relationship with plants through play, by creating an alternative for the current hierarchical, rational way of thinking that eventually led to a disenchantment of the world. Play is an activity that you do for itself, as something pleasurable. With plants you don’t see emotions like play and pleasure, but does that mean that it doesn’t exist?
speaker: Špela Petrič
source: "PL'AI: where plant and machine playfully meet", Waag

title: PL'AI
text: It all got me thinking: What is this humanness that we’re losing? I realized that this kind of humanness, this kind of consideration, is what has also been lacking in our relationship to plants.
speaker: Špela Petrič
source: "In the Algorithm’s Eyes, 'We Are Already Plants'", Getty News (Q&A)

title: PL'AI
text: If I were a plant, I would like an AI robot to be concerned with giving me joy. I don’t want it to improve me, extract from me, or use me to do something that is good for someone else—just play with me.
speaker: Špela Petrič
source: "In the Algorithm’s Eyes, 'We Are Already Plants'", Getty News (Q&A)

title: PL'AI
text: PL’AI, the third work from Špela Petrič’s opus PLANT-MACHINE, embraces the notion of a play as an ontological condition of all living bodies, including plants. The act of playing, unlike games, which are limited by clear rules or goals, reflects the curiosity of existence and is therefore at the heart of (self)knowing.
speaker: Špela Petrič (project text)
source: PL'AI — project page, spelapetric.org

title: Pocket Money
text: Towards the end of making that work I became interested in looking more at young people entering the work force and how their own working shapes their lives.
speaker: Emmaline Zanelli
source: Walter Marsh, ''Hundreds of hours': Honouring the art of labour at the Adelaide Biennial', InReview / InDaily, 17 April 2026

title: Pocket Money
text: I was first interested in what people spend their money on, because it’s something that a lot of people remember – what they spent their own money on when they had their first income,
speaker: Emmaline Zanelli
source: Walter Marsh, ''Hundreds of hours': Honouring the art of labour at the Adelaide Biennial', InReview / InDaily, 17 April 2026

title: Pocket Money
text: But during the process of working with the young people who contributed to the project, some other more nuanced questions about value, time and identity arose.
speaker: Emmaline Zanelli
source: Walter Marsh, ''Hundreds of hours': Honouring the art of labour at the Adelaide Biennial', InReview / InDaily, 17 April 2026

title: Pocket Money
text: Many of the young people in the work spoke about their anxiety about the cost of living, and many of them expressed confusion about how they would ever be able to afford to buy a house in the future.
speaker: Emmaline Zanelli
source: Walter Marsh, ''Hundreds of hours': Honouring the art of labour at the Adelaide Biennial', InReview / InDaily, 17 April 2026

title: Pocket Money
text: There's joy in it, but there's also a sense of it being a bit of a life sentence,
speaker: Emmaline Zanelli
source: AAP, 'Showcase reveals artworks stretched to the outer limits', 26 February 2026

title: Pollinator Pathmaker
text: I’m not offering a technofix. It’s a problem so vast, caused by human destruction of habitats, pollution of ecosystems, and creation of climate change. Pollinator Pathmaker is about transforming our perception of the natural world and giving participants the agency to care for it, rather than consume it.
speaker: Alexandra Daisy Ginsberg
source: Alex Estorick, 'Living Artwork', interview with Alexandra Daisy Ginsberg, Right Click Save, 25 November 2024

title: Pollinator Pathmaker
text: Pollinator Pathmaker is rooted in my ongoing question about whether it’s even possible to make truly altruistic technologies.
speaker: Alexandra Daisy Ginsberg

text: You cannot hoard life, only share it.
speaker: Amelia Winger-Bearskin
source: Text of the work (SKY/WORLD), as quoted in the Whitney press release reprinted by Artdaily, 2022

title: SKY/WORLD DEATH/WORLD
text: These are all just new ways to describe how I use emerging technologies to carry forth the wisdom and stories of our ancestors to make them relevant for the next generation.
speaker: Amelia Winger-Bearskin
source: Cultural Survival, 'The Antecedent Future: Using Emerging Technologies to Carry Forth Wisdom of the Ancestors' (interview by Cristina Verán)

title: SKY/WORLD DEATH/WORLD
text: I use new kinds of technology to tell new kinds of stories. Specifically, I'm interested in science storytelling around environmental futures.
speaker: Amelia Winger-Bearskin
source: Artist Statement 2023, quoted on Signals (DigiBC) page for I Would Like to be Midnight I Would Like to be Sky

title: SMOG SEASON
text: SMOG SEASON invites audiences to realize the bad effect of PM 2.5 they are living in and to start questioning about the problem. Nowadays people start to misunderstand and try to adapt themselves to stay with the problem just like it is a normal weather condition. If we count the problem of PM 2.5 as a season, it would be a very bad monsoon that people must suffer and endure to pass.
speaker: Witaya Junma
source: Witaya Junma, artist website, 'Smog Season'

title: SMOG SEASON
text: "What do we breathe in?" The work wishes to expand on the point of PM 2.5 in Thailand. It is expanding into a chronic problem that is not solved. The work wants to stimulate the thoughts so that everyone returns to look at this problem seriously and question on the right to receive clean air for breathing.
speaker: Witaya Junma
source: Witaya Junma, artist website, 'Smog Season'

title: SMOG SEASON
text: The interesting thing is that this problem does not occur only in Thailand. Many countries around the world are facing air pollution problems, and people must directly take on the burden of the consequences.
speaker: Witaya Junma
source: Witaya Junma, artist website, 'Smog Season'

title: SMOG SEASON
text: Smog Season aims to stimulate thoughts about the chronic air pollution problem in Thailand and encourages people to question their right to breathe clean air.
speaker: Witaya Junma (catalogue text)
source: Prix Ars Electronica Archive, SMOG SEASON, catalogue text

title: Smoke and Mirrors
text: Smoke and Mirrors is about visualising not just the methane data (smoke) in a way people can really absorb but also the disinformation campaign (mirrors) which has caused the data to be denied, doubted and delayed through the decades.
speaker: Beatie Wolfe
source: Statement of Intent, Smoke and Mirrors (beatiewolfe.com)

title: Smoke and Mirrors
text: Realising that a crucial piece of the climate puzzle (how we got to this critical point) has been the fossil fuel industry’s response to the emerging environmental awareness of the 1970s, and that methane emissions (30 times more potent than carbon for trapping heat) are increasingly linked with that industry, I wanted to illuminate this key parallel timeline.
speaker: Beatie Wolfe
source: Statement of Intent, Smoke and Mirrors (beatiewolfe.com)

title: Smoke and Mirrors
text: The ‘smoke and mirrors’ tactics of the big oil industry (and many political bodies and corporations) are so hard to grasp, which leaves a lot of people feeling disempowered, so I wanted this project to help make this slippery reality visible and tangible.
speaker: Beatie Wolfe
source: Hannah Bachl, "From Blue Marble to Bioplastic Record", Ars Electronica Blog, 17 June 2024

title: Smoke and Mirrors
text: It is very important to me that anyone can see the work and immediately get a sense of what they’re viewing
speaker: Beatie Wolfe
source: Hannah Bachl, "From Blue Marble to Bioplastic Record", Ars Electronica Blog, 17 June 2024

title: Smoke and Mirrors
text: In both cases I feel that the music, lyrics etc. really help to bring the data and message to life, to make it feelable and relatable via art’s emotive power.
speaker: Beatie Wolfe
source: Hannah Bachl, "From Blue Marble to Bioplastic Record", Ars Electronica Blog, 17 June 2024

title: Soft Collision
text: Soft Collision (2024) looks at the potential of safe physical interaction by embracing collision rather than avoiding it. Creating a tangible interface between humans and robots as a tool for direct manipulation and live programming.
speaker: Anna Schaeffner
source: Artist website, Soft Collision

title: Soft Collision
text: The Soft Collision project subverted this event by exploring it as an alternative means of communication between human and robot.
speaker: Anna Schaeffner
source: Schaeffner, 'Soft Collision', abstract for Drôles d'objets 2025, Lannion (translated from French)

title: Soft Collision
text: Thus, the energy involved in a collision creates a deformation of matter, which itself becomes the interaction.
speaker: Anna Schaeffner
source: Schaeffner, 'Soft Collision', abstract for Drôles d'objets 2025, Lannion (translated from French)

title: Soft Collision
text: The communicative potential of the material calls for other forms of intelligence through body language.
speaker: Anna Schaeffner
source: Schaeffner, 'Soft Collision', abstract for Drôles d'objets 2025, Lannion (translated from French)

title: Solwata
text: The ocean that’s consuming their world is the same ocean that connects us all. We created this mixed reality installation to collapse that distance.
speaker: Felix Gaedtke, Gayatri Parameswaran (NowHere Media)
source: La Biennale di Venezia, Venice Immersive 2026 — Main Creators' Statement (NowHere Media - Felix Gaedtke, Gayatri Parameswaran)

title: Solwata
text: It forces a reckoning: what is your position in this? What will you do when these changes arrive at your door? That’s the question we want audiences to sit with.
speaker: Felix Gaedtke, Gayatri Parameswaran (NowHere Media)
source: La Biennale di Venezia, Venice Immersive 2026 — Main Creators' Statement (NowHere Media - Felix Gaedtke, Gayatri Parameswaran)

title: Solwata
text: One moment from our trip stays with us – diving underwater to see the remains of the submerged island of Walande, which was once home to a thriving community, now entirely displaced due to rising sea levels. It was sobering, and struck us deeply: this could be all our futures.
speaker: Felix Gaedtke, Gayatri Parameswaran (NowHere Media)
source: La Biennale di Venezia, Venice Immersive 2026 — Main Creators' Statement (NowHere Media - Felix Gaedtke, Gayatri Parameswaran)

title: Solwata
text: Climate change can feel overwhelming because it's often discussed in abstract terms. We wanted to make it tangible by showing what it means for individual people and families.
speaker: Felix Gaedtke
source: Climate Week NYC, 'Environmental justice starts with people: How Solwata brings climate displacement into focus' (interview)

title: Solwata
text: Our goal is for these voices to be heard by the people who have the power to act.
speaker: Gayatri Parameswaran
source: Climate Week NYC, 'Environmental justice starts with people: How Solwata brings climate displacement into focus' (interview)

title: Songs for dying
text: It started out as this research project on animistic and shamanic traditions in different countries and places that were colonised, where you can kind of trace the effects and the built-up trauma.
speaker: Korakrit Arunanondchai
source: The Art Newspaper, 'Korakrit Arunanondchai: on loss, shamanism—and denim' (24 Sept 2021)

title: Songs for dying
text: Most of Songs for dying was shot on the beach where my grandfather raised me in Thailand. When he was cremated, his bones turned to coral, and I went out on a boat and returned them to the sea.
speaker: Korakrit Arunanondchai
source: The Art Newspaper, 'Korakrit Arunanondchai: on loss, shamanism—and denim' (24 Sept 2021)

title: Songs for dying
text: It was hard to tell exactly the moment he died, or what was actually gone. If there was a spirit, when did the spirit leave the body? I was just thinking about shamans using songs as mediums, or even the idea of songs as a method for gathering and transcending to a higher power or this transcendent space.
speaker: Korakrit Arunanondchai
source: The Art Newspaper, 'Korakrit Arunanondchai: on loss, shamanism—and denim' (24 Sept 2021)

title: Songs for dying
text: In Songs for Dying , one of the central ideas is decomposition. I talk about ghosts themselves as decomposers: how they digest ancestral memories, trauma, things that seem like they can’t be processed in one person’s lifetime.
speaker: Korakrit Arunanondchai
source: The White Review, interview with Korakrit Arunanondchai (2021)

title: Songs for dying
text: In Songs for Dying , the membrane becomes the ghost: an embodiment of the space between disparate locations or events where ideas or emotions get translated.
speaker: Korakrit Arunanondchai
source: The White Review, interview with Korakrit Arunanondchai (2021)

title: Sonic Inheritances
artist: Singing Wells (Ketebul Music and Abubilla Music)
text: Our goal is to record, archive and share the traditional music of East Africa for two important reasons – to sustain and celebrate the extraordinary cultural music heritage of the region and to help make this legacy relevant and fresh to today’s audiences.
speaker: Singing Wells
source: Singing Wells, 'Mission'

title: Sonic Inheritances
artist: Singing Wells (Ketebul Music and Abubilla Music)
text: As a group of sound and video engineers, producers and musicians, we set out on this mission not to become ‘fossil collectors’ and store the recordings in inaccessible archives. We work with musicians to make sure their music traditions continue to be practiced, can be shared amongst the widest audiences and become a source of inspiration for new musicians.
speaker: Singing Wells
source: Singing Wells, 'Mission'

title: Sonic Inheritances
artist: Singing Wells (Ketebul Music and Abubilla Music)
text: Singing Wells can’t be just about archiving. We can’t be fossil collectors. We also have to make sure we can bring these traditions into modern music.
speaker: Steve Kivutia, Ketebul Music
source: Singing Wells, 'What We Do'

title: Sonic Inheritances
artist: Singing Wells (Ketebul Music and Abubilla Music)
text: We are committed to supporting traditional music performance in rural East Africa as we believe that this not only serves to promote and preserve the cultural heritage of a community but is also a key indicator of the sustainability of that community.
speaker: Singing Wells
source: Singing Wells, 'What We Do'

title: Speak Slowly and It Will Become a Song
text: Before the work for Aichi was decided, I had the chance to hear a lecture by Kim HeyJung, a researcher of Korean folk songs, and I became interested in women's folk songs. Unlike men's, women's folk songs are said to be characterised by carrying the story of one's own life in the song. I thought it was wonderful how narration becomes melody and turns into music, and I wondered what meaning such folk songs have in the present day.
speaker: Kwon Byungjun
source: BRUTUS.jp, 'Korean Cultural News' Vol.22 Artist Kwon Byungjun (translated from Japanese)

title: Speak Slowly and It Will Become a Song
text: I think it is music that still has meaning today, and the spirit and significance that folk songs carry are wonderful, so I want to introduce them to young people.
speaker: Kwon Byungjun
source: BRUTUS.jp, 'Korean Cultural News' Vol.22 Artist Kwon Byungjun (translated from Japanese)

title: Speak Slowly and It Will Become a Song
text: In Seto City, I asked women in their 60s and 70s to improvise songs of their own lives and sing them.
speaker: Kwon Byungjun
source: BRUTUS.jp, 'Korean Cultural News' Vol.22 Artist Kwon Byungjun (translated from Japanese)

title: Speak Slowly and It Will Become a Song
text: At the venue, you put on headphones I made, fitted with an original high-precision GPS antenna, and as you walk across the wide space you can experience more than 360 different soundscapes. You hear songs, starting with folk songs, and narration, and the areas around them are filled with background sounds of the folk songs as interpreted by AI.
speaker: Kwon Byungjun
source: BRUTUS.jp, 'Korean Cultural News' Vol.22 Artist Kwon Byungjun (translated from Japanese)

title: Spray and Pray
text: It examines how digital media infrastructures produce belief, working through a speculative documentary form that reconstructs automated news networks and algorithmic content systems. Rather than documenting single events, the film stages the mechanisms through which credibility is manufactured.
speaker: Veneta Androva
source: ArtReview, Venice Biennale: Artist Q&As (Bulgaria), 28 May 2026

title: Spray and Pray
text: Spray and Pray works within these ‘minor’ zones – the background infrastructures, automated protocols and algorithmically amplified signals that shape collective imagination. Rather than focusing on visible events, the film examines the conditions that make certain narratives persuasive.
speaker: Veneta Androva
source: ArtReview, Venice Biennale: Artist Q&As (Bulgaria), 28 May 2026

title: Spray and Pray
text: The film treats their outputs not as evidence, but as unstable readings, surfaces that expose the limits, biases, and ambiguities of automated interpretation.
speaker: Veneta Androva
source: Spray and Pray, work page, venetaandrova.com

title: Spray and Pray
text: The tension between raw documentary trace and reconstructed mediation mirrors the very conditions the film investigates: an informational environment in which authenticity is perpetually produced, circulated, and destabilized.
speaker: Veneta Androva
source: Spray and Pray, work page, venetaandrova.com

title: Spray and Pray
text: In Spray and Pray, speculation becomes a form of evidence, tracing opaque infrastructures in which agency, authorship, and responsibility are continuously displaced.
speaker: Veneta Androva
source: Catalogue text, Prix Ars Electronica Archive 2026

title: Stained
text: The film takes place in the narrative world of Mojo, a fictional future I created as a way of bridging the disparities between the contemporary Black experience and landscape discourse. It is a response to my experience in landscape architecture where we were taught to see, study, and interpret landscapes from a limited point of view.
speaker: Jeremy Kamal
source: Ars Electronica Archive — Stained (Prix Ars Electronica 2024)

title: Stained
text: It embraces the friction and harmony that emerges when green agendas (climate activism, environmentalism, ecological study) and contemporary Black experience collide. In their collision, I mine for new rituals, mythologies, and landscapes that challenge our conventional understanding of "nature" and space.
speaker: Jeremy Kamal
source: Ars Electronica Archive — Stained (Prix Ars Electronica 2024)

title: Stained
text: A reason why I took the topic of gang culture is because I particularly did not want to stray away from all aspects of what we deal with in Black life,
speaker: Jeremy Kamal
source: UCSB HFA — Mojo: When Black Identity Shapes the Earth (talk report, 2023)

title: Stained
text: There are opportunities to redefine and reframe these things in a new context, that can take them out of these narratives that we see them through today, and look at them as opportunities for the future.
speaker: Jeremy Kamal
source: UCSB HFA — Mojo: When Black Identity Shapes the Earth (talk report, 2023)

title: Stained
text: Often when we talk about Blackness, the conversation orbits around political systems and social systems, but never around natural ones.
speaker: Jeremy Kamal
source: UCSB HFA — Mojo: When Black Identity Shapes the Earth (talk report, 2023)

title: Still Life: Icon and Fetish (manifestation 1)
text: Positing the question, can machines be taught aesthetics, here the artist trains a machine to look at thousands of still-life paintings, some in their entirety, and some in their details, to try and guide a machine to learn both composition and the painterly nuances of aesthetic.
speaker: Harshit Agrawal
source: (Un)Still Life- Icon and Fetish, artist's website

title: Still Life: Icon and Fetish (manifestation 1)
text: In any painting what is the relation of the part (as fetish) to the whole (as icon)? How can one teach a computer compositional structure and painterly texture? This work tries to start poking into these set of questions.
speaker: Harshit Agrawal
source: (Un)Still Life- Icon and Fetish, artist's website (archival print on canvas)

title: Still Life: Icon and Fetish (manifestation 1)
text: For the second AI, the learning rate is kept fast since the attempt is for the machine to learn abstracted visuals from the dataset - the painterly as opposed to the compositional of the first. Thus, experimenting with both treatments of the dataset and the AI learning process, a new study in aesthetics of icon and fetish emerges.
speaker: Harshit Agrawal
source: STIR, 'Harshit Agrawal's Exo-stential is India's first solo artificial intelligence art show' (interview by Rahul Kumar), 5 October 2021

title: Still Life: Icon and Fetish (manifestation 1)
text: Beyond the conceptual, I am interested in exploring the evolution of aesthetics too enabled by the process of teaching machines a visual language from given examples and varying the training process to produce different visual outcomes, like in Still Life: Icon and Fetish .
speaker: Harshit Agrawal
source: STIR, 'Harshit Agrawal's Exo-stential is India's first solo artificial intelligence art show' (interview by Rahul Kumar), 5 October 2021

title: Still Life: Icon and Fetish (manifestation 1)
text: Having said that, what is fascinating with AI art for the human artist to engage with is - even when machines look at human-labelled human-curated objects (datasets), the generalisations they form (or the patterns they learn from it) are profoundly alien.
speaker: Harshit Agrawal
source: STIR, 'Harshit Agrawal's Exo-stential is India's first solo artificial intelligence art show' (interview by Rahul Kumar), 5 October 2021

title: Stories from the Earth
text: My practice is one of storytelling. It's about the message rather than just the materiality of the work.
speaker: Helena Uambembe
source: PAPER – in conversation with Helena Uambembe 2024/2025 (Nisha Merit)

title: Stories from the Earth
text: So my practice is me looking at how global history and politics are personal and domestic, because that's how I came to exist and how my community came to Pomfret which is connected to global history and politics
speaker: Helena Uambembe
source: PAPER – in conversation with Helena Uambembe 2024/2025 (Nisha Merit)

title: Stories from the Earth
text: And in order for it not to sit and drive me crazy, I had to find ways around it. I was lucky to have worked with Teresa Kutala Fermino [Johannesburg based multimedia artists, who grew up in Pomfret during the same time] and we found ways to deal with that together through writing fairy tales. And from there I continued to write stories but I made them fun.
speaker: Helena Uambembe
source: PAPER – in conversation with Helena Uambembe 2024/2025 (Nisha Merit)

title: Stories from the Earth
text: There was a time I described myself as a storykeeper because I have these archives I would love to make accessible to my community.
speaker: Helena Uambembe
source: PAPER – in conversation with Helena Uambembe 2024/2025 (Nisha Merit)

title: Subnormal Europe
text: Quoting the text of the agreement between the parties, “the main purpose of this initiative is the exact technical reproduction of those instants, which have marked our history of progress in the audiovisual field. The collection must be composed by a set of files, which may be exhibited together with their originals, not being able to distinguish one from the other.”
speaker: Óscar Escudero & Belenish Moreno-Gil (project text)
source: Catalogue text, Prix Ars Electronica 2021 archive

title: Subnormal Europe
text: The team, in cooperation with the Zentrum für Kunst und Medien Karlsruhe, will face the challenge of creating live replicas of these fragments in each of the performances.
speaker: Óscar Escudero & Belenish Moreno-Gil (project text)
source: Catalogue text, Prix Ars Electronica 2021 archive

title: Subnormal Europe
text: The outcomes of the process will be eventually compiled and stored by the EU in order to fulfill the goals of the project, among them, and quoting again the award agreement: “to take the pulse of the current state of the European values and to reaffirm the sense of citizenship of its inhabitants, as well as the knowledge of our common history and its contributions to human development in difficult times for Europeanism.”
speaker: Óscar Escudero & Belenish Moreno-Gil (project text)
source: Catalogue text, Prix Ars Electronica 2021 archive

title: Subnormal Europe
text: Óscar Escudero & Belenish Moreno-Gil (ES) are a couple of transmedia composers and performers whose productions point on social networks as ideology and the creation of operative artistic devices within a “SPAM reality.”
speaker: Óscar Escudero & Belenish Moreno-Gil (biography)
source: Biography, Prix Ars Electronica 2021 archive

title: Sunshine Monument
text: This is an interesting time to be a digital artist. I feel myself bordering multiple dystopias and utopias simultaneously – some of them are technological, some of them are biological, and some of them are social.
speaker: Peter Burr
source: 150 Media Stream, 'Interview with Peter Burr' (on THE CONTINUOUS MONUMENT)

title: Sunshine Monument
text: As an artist, my job is to put form to those borders and potentially conjure something that is present but invisible otherwise.
speaker: Peter Burr
source: 150 Media Stream, 'Interview with Peter Burr' (on THE CONTINUOUS MONUMENT)

title: Sunshine Monument
text: In choosing this technical path, I also leaned into the ambient nature of the space and built an artwork that can run infinitely without repetition.
speaker: Peter Burr
source: 150 Media Stream, 'Interview with Peter Burr' (on THE CONTINUOUS MONUMENT)

title: System's Void
text: It was more of a conceptual idea to record the Earth and shift the perspective away from the human. I wanted to explore what the Earth “hears” when a pipe goes through it or when a well is constantly pumping and extracting gas.
speaker: Sung Tieu
source: The Brooklyn Rail, 'Sung Tieu with Amelia Saul', In Conversation, July/August 2023

title: System's Void
text: Essentially, everything I’ve done is reveal publicly available information that would otherwise require considerable time and effort to uncover.
speaker: Sung Tieu
source: The Brooklyn Rail, 'Sung Tieu with Amelia Saul', In Conversation, July/August 2023

title: System's Void
text: But at the same time, the individual chemicals involved in fracking are poorly understood.
speaker: Sung Tieu
source: The Brooklyn Rail, 'Sung Tieu with Amelia Saul', In Conversation, July/August 2023

title: System's Void
text: Fracking is widespread and widely accepted in the United States, to the point where it becomes challenging to argue against it because it has become deeply ingrained in the fabric of the country and its workforce.
speaker: Sung Tieu
source: The Brooklyn Rail, 'Sung Tieu with Amelia Saul', In Conversation, July/August 2023

title: Taala Village
text: From the immersive world of gaming at hand, the artist retreats to proto-design ideas of early game building with minimal pixels. His characters are mobilized through Sri Lankan music instruments and sonic layering. Visitors are invited to venture into a virtual island where echoes, whispers, chimes, and vibrations accompany each action sequence.
speaker: unattributed (festival publication text)
source: Colomboscope 2026: Rhythm Alliances, exhibition publication (eds. Natasha Ginwala and Hajra Haider Karrar), p. 46

title: Taala Village
text: Taala Village exemplifies Abeysinghe's practice of developing video gaming as a wayfinding technique in cultural storytelling.
speaker: unattributed (festival publication text)
source: Colomboscope 2026: Rhythm Alliances, exhibition publication (eds. Natasha Ginwala and Hajra Haider Karrar), p. 46

title: TAFAA – Fertility Device (Uncanny Valley)
text: For me it is very important not to be positive or negative. I am not looking to pass judgment or be prescriptive. As an artist, my interests are first and foremost to produce a particular aesthetic in relation to my reflections and think about how my work affects the audience by stimulating the different human senses.
speaker: Chloé Delarue
source: Sara Harrison, "Chloé Delarue: Art and the humanity of tech", Julius Baer Art Collection

title: TAFAA – Fertility Device (Uncanny Valley)
text: drifting into simulated environments to observe the transformation of reality as it is filtered by the appearance of immediacy
speaker: Chloé Delarue
source: Sara Harrison, "Chloé Delarue: Art and the humanity of tech", Julius Baer Art Collection (her own term for her working process, quoted in the article)

title: TALK SHOW
text: I see the form of reenactment or remaking as an ingredient in the work that functions as a vessel to pour other ideas into. It interests me how a reenactment is a new event in itself.
speaker: Jordan Strafer
source: Marie de Brugerolle, 'Liminal Systems of Representation. A Conversation with Jordan Strafer', Flash Art (2023)

title: TALK SHOW
text: A video work on loop in a gallery isn’t that different from a TV playing a soap opera or a trial in the background. The form permits you to tune in and out.
speaker: Jordan Strafer
source: Marie de Brugerolle, 'Liminal Systems of Representation. A Conversation with Jordan Strafer', Flash Art (2023)

title: TALK SHOW
text: The storyline in LOOPHOLE is the result of my contemplation over the incompatibility of the justice system and a rape trial. I just don’t see any possibility of a resolution between those two things. The system itself is built on violence.
speaker: Jordan Strafer
source: Marie de Brugerolle, 'Liminal Systems of Representation. A Conversation with Jordan Strafer', Flash Art (2023)

title: Templo da água: rio Tietê
text: circularity of healing created by sound itself—sound that heals [by offering us] the possibility of participating in creating reality, the desire to live, to energize our bodies, and stir up movement
speaker: Leonel Vásquez
source: Quoted in Lisa Blackmore, 'When the River Summons… Poetic Hydraulics and Aquatic Enchantments', curatorial text for Templo del agua, NC ARTE, Bogotá, 2023 (English version; brackets are the curator's; about the Río Bogotá version)

title: Templo da água: rio Tietê
text: But when you start to listen to it, you realise that it isn't so. The river has life. There are anaerobic bacteria that consume material and carry out processes of release
speaker: Leonel Vásquez
source: Radio Nacional de Colombia, 'Escuchar el río y conectar con la vida que está en el agua' (Violetta Ramirez Bermudez), on Templo del Agua: Río Bogotá (translated from Spanish)

title: Templo da água: rio Tietê
text: It's like putting vocal cords on the rivers
speaker: Leonel Vásquez
source: Radio Nacional de Colombia, 'Escuchar el río y conectar con la vida que está en el agua', on his 'amphibious lutherie' devices used in Templo del Agua (translated from Spanish)

title: Templo da água: rio Tietê
text: In this project I am interested in working with these kinds of sensations, and with them on the well-being of the minds of those who attend, because that is where the imbalance operates in the instrumental thinking that has understood nature, and within it the waters, as inert matter.
speaker: Leonel Vásquez
source: Leonel Vásquez, artist website, 'Templo del Agua Sumapaz' project text (translated from Spanish)

title: Templo da água: rio Tietê
text: It arises from the need to have a space to re-value the waters in which our life flows daily, from the need for a time of intimacy, to allow ourselves to receive the healing vibration of water, a sacred space, a space to express gratitude and to shelter in the blessing and compassion of nature.
speaker: Leonel Vásquez
source: Leonel Vásquez, artist website, 'Templo del Agua Sumapaz' project text (translated from Spanish)

title: Temporary Stored
text: Archives have always been framed in a guise that promotes a Western perspective of representations of the Other, a modernity in which the institutions and museums frame these archives and collections.
speaker: Joseph Kamaru (project statement)
source: Prix Ars Electronica 2023, project page

title: Temporary Stored
text: Written sources in the West are deemed ontologically concrete and immune to individual distortion, whereas oral sources seem nebulous and subjectively constituted.
speaker: Joseph Kamaru (project statement)
source: Prix Ars Electronica 2023, project page

title: Temporary Stored
text: These are historical carriers, spiritual beings, and cultural entities that have been passed over generations and are meant to be learned from and act as reflections of past and future histories.
speaker: Joseph Kamaru (project statement)
source: Kunstradio (Ö1), Radiokunst, 23 July 2023

title: Temporary Stored
text: I realized that museums also store sound, rather than only objects. I felt that I needed to explore that, because the museums mostly made the recordings only accessible to researchers.
speaker: KMRU (Joseph Kamaru)
source: Subbacultcha, “An interview with KMRU”

title: Temporary Stored
text: For Temporary Stored I was trying to make an archive film with sound, and engage in the discourse of repatriation.
speaker: KMRU (Joseph Kamaru)
source: Subbacultcha, “An interview with KMRU”

title: Thank you for your souvenir, UK!

title: Thank you for your souvenir, UK!

title: Unknown Label
text: It is a video installation that deals with the human labour involved in training AI systems, and more specifically with the training of self-driving vehicles in order to "read" their environment, that is recognizing elements around a car when it's driving itself. The process is called "image segmentation" and it consists of drawing an outline around every object in a given image of a street and put a label on it. It is basically translating our world to be machine-readable.
speaker: Nicolas Gourault
source: In Dialogue: Artist Talk with werkleitz, EMAP / emare.eu

title: Unknown Label
text: It was uncanny to discover this whole process of human labour which is hidden behind a cover of so-called intelligent algorithms. Far from the narrative of the technological breakthrough, there is still until now a very old school system that relies on the inequalities of the global economy in order to enable the AI systems that we benefit from in our daily lives.
speaker: Nicolas Gourault
source: In Dialogue: Artist Talk with werkleitz, EMAP / emare.eu

title: Unknown Label

It was very special to feel that through their gaze I gained a different perspective on our own world and its own artificiality.
speaker: Nicolas Gourault

title: Unknown Label
text: It was important to build some trust with these people because everything is taking place online, there is a lot of fear about scam or abuse because the workers on this platform don't know their clients, they don't know who they're exactly working for. Everything is very opaque, and there is always this fear of not getting the money at the end of the week.

title: Unknown Label
text: Unknown Label reveals the hidden crowd that works with these operational images and help shape how machines see the world. A digital collage, layering together fragments of annotated images and a virtual map of the world as seen by self-driving cars, creates a space where the viewers can share the vision of otherwise invisible data workers. The video installation thus raises the question of how to reappropriate these operational images which depict and categorize the world we live in without our prior knowledge or agreement.
speaker: Nicolas Gourault (project description)
source: Unknown Label (2023) / Their Eyes (2025), EMAP work page
